## Overview

In this module we demonstrate how to combine and split DataFrames.

## Combining and Splitting DataFrames

* Spark SQL supports the usual database-style joins:
    * Cross join
    * Inner join
    * Left semi join
    * Left anti join
    * Left outer join
    * Right outer join
    * Full outer join

* Joins are expensive in the big-data world
    * Perform joins early in the process
    * Amortize the cost over many use cases

* Spark SQL supports the following set operations:
    * Union
    * Intersection
    * Subtraction

* Spark SQL provides a method to split a DataFrame into random subsets

## Joining DataFrames

paragraphs.title: We will use the following DataFrames to demonstrate joins
paragraphs.text:
%pyspark

scientists = spark.read.csv("/duocar/raw/data_scientists/", header=True, inferSchema=True)
scientists.show()

offices = spark.read.csv("/duocar/raw/offices/", header=True, inferSchema=True)
offices.show()

paragraphs.title: Cross join
paragraphs.text:
%pyspark

# Use the `crossJoin` DataFrame method to join every row in the left (`scientists`) DataFrame with every row in the right (`offices`) DataFrame:
scientists.crossJoin(offices).show()

paragraphs.title: Warning
paragraphs.text:
%md
This can result in very big DataFrames!

paragraphs.title: Note
paragraphs.text:
%md
Columns with the same name are not renamed.
This is called the *Cartesian product* of the two DataFrames.

paragraphs.title: Inner join
paragraphs.text:
%pyspark

# Use the `join` DataFrame method with different values of the `how` argument to perform other types of joins

# Use a join expression and the value `inner` to return only those rows for which the join expression is true:
scientists.join(offices, scientists.office_id == offices.office_id, "inner").show()

# This gives us a list of data scientists associated with an office and the corresponding office information.

# Since the join key has the same name on both DataFrames, we can simplify the join as follows:
scientists.join(offices, "office_id", "inner").show()

# Since an inner join is the default, we can further simplify the join as follows:
scientists.join(offices, "office_id").show()

paragraphs.title: Left semi join
paragraphs.text:
%pyspark

# Use the value `left_semi` to return the rows in the left DataFrame that match rows in the right DataFrame:
scientists \
  .join(offices, scientists.office_id == offices.office_id, "left_semi") \
  .show()

# This gives us a list of data scientists associated with an office.

paragraphs.title: Left anti join
paragraphs.text:
%pyspark

# Use the value `left_anti` to return the rows in the left DataFrame that do not match rows in the right DataFrame:
scientists \
  .join(offices, scientists.office_id == offices.office_id, "left_anti") \
  .show()

# This gives us a list of data scientists not associated with an office.

paragraphs.title: Note
paragraphs.text:
%md
You can think of the left semi and left anti joins as special types of filters.

paragraphs.title: Left outer join
paragraphs.text:
%pyspark

# Use the value `left` or `left_outer` to return every row in the left DataFrame with or without matching rows in the right DataFrame:
scientists \
  .join(offices, scientists.office_id == offices.office_id, "left_outer") \
  .show()

# This gives us a list of data scientists with or without an office.

paragraphs.title: Right outer join
paragraphs.text:
%pyspark

# Use the value `right` or `right_outer` to return every row in the right
# DataFrame with or without matching rows in the left DataFrame:
scientists \
  .join(offices, scientists.office_id == offices.office_id, "right_outer") \
  .show()

# This gives us a list of offices with or without a data scientist.

paragraphs.title: Note
paragraphs.text:
%md
The Paris office has two data scientists.

paragraphs.title: Full outer join
paragraphs.text:
%pyspark

# Use the value `full`, `outer`, or `full_outer` to return the union of the left outer and right outer joins (with duplicates removed):
scientists \
  .join(offices, scientists.office_id == offices.office_id, "full_outer") \
  .show()

# This gives us a list of all data scientists whether or not they have an office and all offices whether or not they have any data scientists.

%md
### Example: Joining the DuoCar data

Let us join the driver, rider, and review data with the ride data.

paragraphs.title: Read the clean data from HDFS
paragraphs.text:
%pyspark

rides = spark.read.parquet("/duocar/clean/rides/")
drivers = spark.read.parquet("/duocar/clean/drivers/")
riders = spark.read.parquet("/duocar/clean/riders/")
reviews = spark.read.parquet("/duocar/clean/ride_reviews/")

paragraphs.title: Since we want all the ride data, we will use a sequence of left outer joins
paragraphs.text:
%pyspark

joined = rides \
  .join(drivers, rides.driver_id == drivers.id, "left_outer") \
  .join(riders, rides.rider_id == riders.id, "left_outer") \
  .join(reviews, rides.id == reviews.ride_id, "left_outer")
joined.printSchema()

paragraphs.title: Note
paragraphs.text:
%md
We probably want to rename some columns before joining the data and remove the duplicate ID columns after joining the data to make this DataFrame  more usable.

paragraphs.title: For example, see the `joined` data in the DuoCar data repository
paragraphs.text:
%pyspark

spark.read.parquet("/duocar/joined/").printSchema()

%md

## Applying set operations to DataFrames

Spark SQL provides the following DataFrame methods that implement set operations:
* `union`
* `intersect`
* `subtract`

paragraphs.title: Use the `union` method to get the union of rows in two DataFrames with similar schema
paragraphs.text:
%pyspark

driver_names = drivers.select("first_name")
driver_names.count()

rider_names = riders.select("first_name")
rider_names.count()

names_union = driver_names.union(rider_names).orderBy("first_name")
names_union.count()
names_union.show()

paragraphs.title: Note that `union` does not remove duplicates. Use the `distinct` method to remove duplicates
paragraphs.text:
%pyspark

names_distinct = names_union.distinct()
names_distinct.count()
names_distinct.show()

paragraphs.title: Use the `intersect` method to return rows that exist in both DataFrames
paragraphs.text:
%pyspark

name_intersect = driver_names.intersect(rider_names).orderBy("first_name")
name_intersect.count()
name_intersect.show()

paragraphs.title: Use the `subtract` method to return rows in the left DataFrame that do not exist in the right DataFrame
paragraphs.text:
%pyspark

names_subtract = driver_names.subtract(rider_names).orderBy("first_name")
names_subtract.count()
names_subtract.show()

%md
 ## Splitting a DataFrame

paragraphs.title: Use the `randomSplit` DataFrame method to split a DataFrame into random subsets
paragraphs.text:
%pyspark

riders.count()
(train, validate, test) = riders.randomSplit(weights=[0.6, 0.2, 0.2])

print((train.count(), validate.count(), test.count()))

# Use the `seed` argument to ensure replicability:
(train, validate, test) = riders.randomSplit([0.6, 0.2, 0.2], seed=12345)
print((train.count(), validate.count(), test.count()))

# If the proportions do not add up to one, then Spark will normalize the values:
(train, validate, test) = riders.randomSplit([60.0, 20.0, 20.0], seed=12345)
print((train.count(), validate.count(), test.count()))

paragraphs.title: Note
paragraphs.text:
%md
The weights must be doubles.
The same seed will result in the same random split.

# Lab

paragraphs.title: 1 - Join the `rides` DataFrame with the `reviews` DataFrame.  Keep only those rides that have a review
paragraphs.text:
%pyspark

# Count the number of reviews before the join:
print(reviews.count())

# Perform a right outer join:
rides_with_reviews = rides.join(reviews, rides.id == reviews.ride_id, "right_outer")

# Count the number of reviews after the join:
print(rides_with_reviews.count())

# Print the schema:
rides_with_reviews.printSchema()

paragraphs.title: 2 - How many drivers have not provided a ride?
paragraphs.text:
%pyspark

# Get the driver IDs from `drivers` DataFrame:
id_from_drivers = drivers.select("id")

# Get the driver IDs from `rides` DataFrame:
id_from_rides = rides.select("driver_id").withColumnRenamed("driver_id", "id")

# Find lazy drivers using a left anti join:
lazy_drivers1 = id_from_drivers.join(id_from_rides, "id", "left_anti")
lazy_drivers1.count()
lazy_drivers1.orderBy("id").show(5)

# Find lazy drivers using a subtraction:
lazy_drivers2 = id_from_drivers.subtract(id_from_rides)
